x: In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Commentary on Sūrat al-Mursalāt (Those Sent Forth).
The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘By those sent forth successively
n
, by the storming winds
n
, by those that spread widely
n
, by those that distinguish decisively
n
, and by those that convey a reminder (5), as an excuse or a warning (6).’
The interpreters differed about ‘those sent forth successively.’

Some said they are winds sent one after another. Among those who held this view, Ibn Masʿūd identified them as winds; another report from him gives the same explanation, as does Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Suddī, transmitting from Abū Ṣāliḥ, said they are winds. Mujāhid and Qatādah likewise identified them as winds.

Others said they are angels sent with what is right. Masrūq said those sent forth are angels. A report from ʿAbd Allāh likewise identifies them as angels. Abū Ṣāliḥ said they are messengers sent with what is right, meaning messengers sent with God’s commands and prohibitions.

Some said ʿurfan means ‘in succession,’ like a horse’s mane; Arabs say that people came to someone ‘as one mane’ when they go toward him in large numbers. Ibn Buraydah said it means that one follows another. The sound view, al-Ṭabarī says, is that God swore by those sent forth successively. Angels may be sent in succession, and winds may also be sent in succession. Nothing indicates that one of these two kinds alone is intended, so His oath includes everything possessing the described quality: an angel, a wind, or a human messenger sent forth.
His saying, ‘by the storming winds’: God means the winds that blow violently, with strong and rapid gusts.

The interpreters said similarly. ʿAlī was asked what the storming winds are and answered: the wind. Ibn Masʿūd gave the same explanation. Several reports from Ibn Masʿūd likewise identify them as wind. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Abū Ṣāliḥ also said they are wind or winds. Further reports from ʿAlī, Qatādah, and others identify the storming winds as winds.
His saying, ‘by those that spread widely’: the interpreters differed.

Some said the spreading ones are winds. Ibn Masʿūd identified them as wind; another report from him gives the same explanation. Several reports from Ibn Masʿūd, Mujāhid, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and Qatādah likewise identify them as winds.
Others said they are rain. Abū Ṣāliḥ said they are rain.

Others said they are angels who spread out the records of deeds. Abū Ṣāliḥ said they are angels spreading the records. Al-Ṭabarī considers the sound view to be that God swore by all that spreads something: winds spread clouds, rain spreads across the earth, and angels spread the records. Nothing decisive restricts the meaning to one kind, so it includes everything that spreads.
His saying, ‘by those that distinguish decisively’: the interpreters differed.
Some said these are angels who distinguish truth from falsehood. Abū Ṣāliḥ identified them as angels. A report from Abū Ṣāliḥ and one from Ibn ʿAbbās likewise identify them as angels.

Others said they are the Qur’an. Qatādah said the Qur’an is meant, since God distinguishes truth from falsehood in it. Al-Ṭabarī says the correct view is that these are those who separate truth from falsehood; God has not singled out one kind. His oath therefore includes anything that distinguishes truth from falsehood, whether an angel, the Qur’an, or something else.
His saying, ‘by those that convey a reminder’: they convey God’s revelation to His messengers; they are the angels.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are angels. Qatādah said the angels cast the reminder upon the messengers and convey it. In another report he said they cast down the Qur’an. Sufyān likewise identified them as angels.
His saying, ‘as an excuse or a warning’: the angels convey the reminder to the messengers as God’s means of removing any excuse among His creatures and warning them.

The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said it is an excuse from God and a warning to His creatures. Qatādah said it is a proof against God’s creatures and a warning from Him to believers, who benefit from it and heed it. Ibn ʿAbbās said the phrase refers to angels. Readers differed: most of Medina and Syria, some Meccans, and some Kufans read ‘excuse’ lightly and ‘warning’ with emphasis; most Kufans and some Basrans read both lightly; other Basrans read both with emphasis. Al-Ṭabarī prefers the light forms, while accepting the soundness of the emphatic forms, because both are verbal nouns meaning the removal of excuses and warning.

evidence.text: Readers differed: most of Medina and Syria, some Meccans, and some Kufans read ‘excuse’ lightly and ‘warning’ with emphasis; most Kufans and some Basrans read both lightly; other Basrans read both with emphasis.

x: The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘What you are promised will surely occur (7): when the stars are extinguished (8), when the heaven is split open (9), when the mountains are scattered (10), and when the messengers are appointed for their time (11)—for what Day are they deferred? (12) For the Day of Decision (13). And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is? (14) Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (15).’ God says that what people are promised will certainly come to pass: the Resurrection and the reward and punishment God has prepared for His creatures that Day.

His saying, ‘when the stars are extinguished’: when their light disappears so they have no radiance or brightness … … ‘when the heaven is split open’: when it is cleft and cracked. ‘When the mountains are scattered’: when they are uprooted and dispersed as floating dust. ‘When the messengers are appointed for their time’: when the messengers are deferred until their appointed gathering on the Day of Resurrection.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are gathered. Mujāhid explained it as deferred; Sufyān transmitted the same. Ibrāhīm said they are promised a time. Ibn Zayd said the messengers are appointed for the Day of Resurrection, citing ‘the Day God gathers the messengers’ (Q 5:109), and explaining that an appointed term is a fixed time. He also cited ‘They ask you about the new moons. Say: they are time markers for people and for the pilgrimage’ (Q 2:189), and ‘for the appointed time of a known Day’ (Q 56:50), meaning the Resurrection: they have a term until they reach that Day. Ibrāhīm likewise said they were promised. Readers differed between forms with hamzah and wāw, and between a light or doubled qāf. Al-Ṭabarī says all are established readings and well-known dialect forms with the same meaning: ‘made appointed’ from waqt, time. Some Arabs find initial wāw with ḍammah heavy and replace it with hamzah, as in ujūh for wujūh.
A poet’s verse shows this pronunciation.

evidence.text: Readers differed between forms with hamzah and wāw, and between a light or doubled qāf.

x: His saying, ‘For what Day are they deferred?’ God says this to make His servants marvel at the terror and severity of that Day: for what tremendous and fearsome Day are the messengers deferred and appointed? He then explains: ‘They are deferred for the Day of Decision,’ when God judges between His creatures, gives the wronged person his due from the wrongdoer, and recompenses the good-doer for good and the evildoer for evil. Qatādah said it is the Day when people are judged by their deeds and sent to Paradise or the Fire.

His saying, ‘And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?’ God addresses His Prophet Muḥammad, magnifying the matter and terror of that Day. Qatādah said the expression serves to magnify it.

His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe is a valley in Hell in which the pus of its inhabitants flows. It is for those who deny the Day of Decision. Qatādah said … … ‘Woe indeed is long-lasting.’

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Did We not destroy the earlier peoples (16), then make the later ones follow them (17)? Thus do We deal with the guilty (18). Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (19).’ God says: Did We not destroy the earlier nations who denied Our messengers and rejected Our signs, such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd, and Thamūd? Then We caused later peoples who followed their path of disbelief to follow them, such as the people of Abraham, the people of Lot, and the people of Midian. We destroy them just as We destroyed those before them. This is Our way with criminal nations when they transgress and act arrogantly. Woe that Day to those who deny God’s reports in this verse and reject His power to do whatever He wills.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Did We not create you from a humble fluid (20), then place it in a secure receptacle (21), until a known term (22)? We determined its measure—how excellent are those who determine (23)! Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (24).’ God says: people, did We not create you from a weak drop of fluid? Ibn ʿAbbās explained ‘humble’ as weak.
His saying, ‘then place it in a secure receptacle’: We placed the weak fluid in a womb, where it settled and was firmly lodged.
The interpreters said similarly. Mujāhid explained the secure receptacle as the womb.

His saying, ‘until a known term’: until a time known to God for the fetus to emerge from the womb. Readers differed over ‘We determined’: most Medinan readers doubled the dāl; most Kufan and Basran readers read it lightly. Both are established readings and either is correct, though al-Ṭabarī prefers the lighter form because of ‘how excellent are those who determine.’ Arabs may combine two forms, as in ‘Give the disbelievers respite; grant them a brief respite’ (Q 86:17), which combines a doubled and a light form. The two readings may also have the same meaning, since Arabs say both ‘death was decreed for him’ with a light and doubled form. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk explained ‘We determined its measure—how excellent are those who determine’ as ‘We took possession; how excellent are the possessors.’

evidence.text: Readers differed over ‘We determined’: most Medinan readers doubled the dāl; most Kufan and Basran readers read it lightly.
The two readings may also have the same meaning, since Arabs say both ‘death was decreed for him’ with a light and doubled form.

x: His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe that Day to those who deny that God created them from a humble fluid.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Did We not make the earth a gathering place (25) for the living and the dead (26), place lofty, firm mountains in it, and give you fresh water to drink (27)? Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (28).’ God reminds His servants of His blessings: people, did We not make the earth a container for you? One says that a thing is another’s container when it holds it. The meaning is: did We not make the earth a container for your living and your dead, gathering the living in dwellings and homes and enclosing the dead in its interior graves? It may also mean that it contains what harms people while they live and their corpses after death. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as a shelter. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd found a louse in his garment, buried it in the mosque, and recited, ‘Did We not make the earth a gathering place for the living and the dead?’ Mujāhid said that if someone sees a louse on his clothes while in the mosque, he may throw it away or bury it. Al-Shaʿbī said the earth’s interior is for your dead and its surface for your living. Mujāhid explained that the earth contains what harms people while they live and conceals them when they die; it contains the living and the dead alike. Mujāhid said the living dwell in the earth. They disappear into it wherever they wish.

‘Living and dead’: the dead are buried in it. Qatādah said the living dwell on earth and the dead are buried there. Another report from Qatādah says the living are on its surface and the dead are interred in it. Arab grammarians differed over the accusative ‘living and dead’: some Basrans treated it as a circumstantial phrase; some Kufans said it is governed by ‘container,’ as if one said ‘a container for the living and the dead.’ Al-Ṭabarī considers the latter more correct.

His saying, ‘We placed lofty, firm mountains in it’: God placed firmly rooted, lofty, towering mountains in the earth. Qatādah explained them as mountains. Ibn ʿAbbās explained ‘lofty, firm mountains’ as elevated mountains.

His saying, ‘and gave you fresh water to drink’: We gave you sweet water. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatādah explained furāt as sweet. Ibn ʿAbbās also said it comes from four rivers: the Sayḥān, Jayḥān, Nile, and Euphrates. Every water that a son of Adam drinks comes from these rivers, which issue from beneath a rock near Jerusalem. Sayḥān is in Balkh; Jayḥān is the Tigris; the Euphrates is the Euphrates of Kufa; and the Nile is the Nile of Egypt. … and as for the Nile, it is the Nile of Egypt.
His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe that Day to those who deny these blessings with which I favored you, yet disbelieve in their Creator.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Go to that which you used to deny (29). Go to a shadow with three branches (30), neither giving shade nor protecting from the flame (31). It throws sparks like a palace (32), as if they were yellow camels (33). Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (34).’ God says that on the Day of Resurrection these deniers of the blessings and proofs presented to them will be told: go to the punishment of God that you denied in this world. ‘Go to a shadow with three branches’ means the shadow of smoke with three branches. Smoke rises from the fuel of Hell and then divides into three branches. Mujāhid said it is the smoke of Hell. Qatādah compared it to the enclosure of fire surrounding its inhabitants (Q 18:29). Qatādah said the enclosure is the smoke of the Fire. It surrounds them, then divides into three branches: one here, one there, and one there. Thus God says, ‘Go to a shadow with three branches, neither giving shade nor protecting from the flame.’
His saying, ‘neither giving shade’: it does not shade them from the Fire’s heat. ‘Nor protecting from the flame’ means it does not shelter them from its blaze.
His saying, ‘It throws sparks like a palace’: Hell throws sparks like a palace. The regional readers read qaṣr with a still ṣād. They differed over its meaning.

Some said it means one of the palaces. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as a great palace. Mujāhid likewise said the verse mentions a palace. Al-Quraẓī said that a wall surrounds Hell, and what comes out from beyond it and returns into it is as large as a palace and the color of pitch.

Others said qaṣr means thick pieces of wood, like palm trunks. Ibn ʿAbbās said qaṣr was the name for pieces of wood kept for winter, three cubits long or more or less. Another report says people in the pre-Islamic period cut wood to lengths of a cubit, more or less, and used it as fuel. A further report says they cut pieces two or three cubits long, more or less, and called them qaṣr. Ibn ʿAbbās said qaṣr means cut wood or felled palm trunks. Mujāhid said it means bundles of wood. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, compared the sparks to the trunk of a palm. Qatādah said they are the bases of trees and palms; another report compares them to tree trunks. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said they are great tree trunks, like the middles of yellow camels. The middle of anything is its center, and these are the centers. Al-Ḥasan read it as ‘like a palace’ and said it means a large log; its singular is qaṣrah or qaṣr, like a single ember and embers, or a date and dates.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have read qaṣar with the ṣād vowelled. Another report from him reads it with fatḥah on both qāf and ṣād, and another says it means palm trunks, that is, their necks. Al-Ṭabarī considers the regional reading with a still ṣād the most correct, and the best interpretation is ‘palaces,’ supported by ‘as if they were yellow camels’: Arabs compare camels to built palaces. Al-Akhṭal described a she-camel as ‘like a Roman tower, built firm with plaster, bricks, and stones.’ The verse says ‘sparks like a palace,’ singular rather than ‘palaces.’ The plural can be expressed by a collective singular, as in ‘the army will be defeated and turn their back’ (Q 54:45), where ‘back’ has the sense of ‘backs.’ This construction also suits the verse endings and cadence, as is common in Arabic, the language in which the Qur’an was revealed. ‘Like a palace’ means in the palace’s great size, as in ‘their eyes roll like one overcome by death’ (Q 33:19), where the comparison is to the action, not to a single eye.
Al-Aswad was asked about the verse and said: like a palace.

evidence.text: The regional readers read qaṣr with a still ṣād. They differed over its meaning.
Al-Ḥasan read it as ‘like a palace’ and said it means a large log; its singular is qaṣrah or qaṣr, like a single ember and embers, or a date and dates.
Another report from him reads it with fatḥah on both qāf and ṣād, and another says it means palm trunks, that is, their necks.

Al-Ṭabarī considers the regional reading with a still ṣād the most correct, and the best interpretation is ‘palaces,’ supported by ‘as if they were yellow camels’: Arabs compare camels to built palaces.

x: His saying, ‘as if they were yellow camels’: the interpreters differed.

Some said the sparks thrown by Hell are like large black camels; here ṣufr (‘yellow’) means black. Black camels have a tinge of yellow, so they are called yellow; similarly, gazelles are called udm because darkness covers their whiteness.

Among those who said this … … Al-Ḥasan said they are black camels. Qatādah compared them to the black she-camels people have seen; in another report he said black she-camels. Mujāhid said they are camels.

Others said the phrase refers instead to the thick ropes of ships, to which the sparks are compared. Ibn ʿAbbās said the yellow camel-like forms are ship cables gathered and tied around ships. He described them as sea-ship cables joined together until they are as thick as a man’s waist. Another report gives the same explanation. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said they are bridge cables; he also said they are ropes. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are ropes of sea-going ships. Mujāhid said they are bridge cables.

Others said they are pieces of copper; Ibn ʿAbbās gave that interpretation. Al-Ṭabarī considers the most correct view to be that they are black camels, which is the familiar meaning in Arabic; jamālāt is a plural of jamal, just as rijālāt is a plural of rijāl and buyūtāt a plural of buyūt. Readers differed: most Medinan and Basran readers and some Kufans read jamālāt with a kasrah on the jīm and a tāʾ, as a plural of jamal; it may also be a plural of jamālah, just as stones are a plural of stone. Most Kufan readers also read jamālāt with kasrah on the jīm, interpreting it as a plural of camel, formed through jamālah, like ḥijārah from ḥajar. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have read jumālāt, with ḍammah on the jīm, as a plural of a gathered mass. Al-Ṭabarī says readers may choose either established regional reading with kasrah, whether ending in tāʾ or hāʾ (which becomes tāʾ in connected recitation).
He does not permit the reading with ḍammah on the jīm because the authoritative readers agree against it.

evidence.text: Readers differed: most Medinan and Basran readers and some Kufans read jamālāt with a kasrah on the jīm and a tāʾ, as a plural of jamal; it may also be a plural of jamālah, just as stones are a plural of stone.
Most Kufan readers also read jamālāt with kasrah on the jīm, interpreting it as a plural of camel, formed through jamālah, like ḥijārah from ḥajar.
Al-Ṭabarī says readers may choose either established regional reading with kasrah, whether ending in tāʾ or hāʾ (which becomes tāʾ in connected recitation).
He does not permit the reading with ḍammah on the jīm because the authoritative readers agree against it.

x: His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe on the Day of Resurrection to those who deny the truth. This is the threat God has issued to those among His servants who deny it.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘This is a Day on which they will not speak (35), nor will they be granted permission to offer excuses (36). Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (37). This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the earlier peoples (38). If you have a plan, then use it against Me (39). Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (40).’ God says to those who deny His reward and punishment: this is a Day on which they will not speak to deny either. They will not be permitted to offer excuses for the sins they committed in this world.

Someone might ask how God can say ‘This is a Day on which they will not speak’ when He reports that they say ‘Our Lord, take us out of it’ (Q 23:107), and ‘Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice’ (Q 40:11), among other statements reported from them by God and His Messenger.
that they speak in some states of that Day, but not in others.

His saying, ‘This is a Day on which they will not speak’ reports that they will be silent during some states of that Day, not throughout the entire Day. The proof is that ‘Day’ is connected to ‘they will not speak.’ Arabs connect ‘day’ to a past- or present-tense verb when they mean a particular hour or time within the day. For example, ‘I will come to you on the day so-and-so arrives’ means at the time he arrives, not throughout the whole day. This construction is used when ‘day’ means ‘when’ or ‘whenever,’ which take verbs rather than nouns.

‘Then they will offer excuses’ is in the nominative, coordinated with ‘nor will they be granted permission.’ This was chosen over the subjunctive despite the preceding negation because it ends a verse and matches the other verse endings. The subjunctive would also be permissible, as in ‘Their punishment will not be lightened so that they may die’ (Q 35:36). Both nominative and subjunctive forms are valid, as in ‘Who is it that will lend God a good loan, so that He may multiply it for him?’ (Q 2:245), which is read in both ways.

evidence.text: (Q 2:245), which is read in both ways.

x: His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe that Day to those who deny God’s report about these people and what He will do to them on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, ‘This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the earlier peoples’: God tells those who deny resurrection that this is the Day on which He will justly judge between His servants. ‘We have gathered you and the earlier peoples’ means that We gathered you for the meeting We promised in this world, when you and the nations before you would be assembled. We have fulfilled that promise. ‘If you have a plan, then use it against Me’ means: God will fulfill His promise of punishment for your denial that you would be raised on this Day. If you have any stratagem to escape His punishment today, then try it.
His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe that Day to those who deny this report.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘The God-fearing will be amid shades and springs (41), and fruits of whatever they desire (42). “Eat and drink pleasantly for what you used to do” (43). Thus do We reward those who excel in good (44). Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (45).’ God says those who feared His punishment by fulfilling His obligations and avoiding disobedience in this world will be in cooling shades and sheltered cover, untouched by harm from heat or cold. This contrasts with the disbelievers’ three-branched shade that gives no shade and no protection from flame. They will also be among springs—rivers flowing through the trees of their gardens—and fruits of whatever they desire, eating without fear of harm or unpleasant consequences.

His saying, ‘Eat and drink pleasantly for what you used to do’: they will be told, ‘Eat from these fruits and drink from these springs whatever you desire, pleasantly.’ Nothing will spoil or disturb what they eat and drink; it will remain for them forever and will be wholesome, causing no bodily harm.
His saying, ‘for what you used to do’: they will be told that this is a reward for the obedience they practiced in this world and for striving in what brings them near to God.

His saying, ‘Thus do We reward those who excel in good’: just as We rewarded these God-fearing people for obeying Us in this world with the recompense described, We likewise reward and recompense those who excel in obeying and worshipping Us. We do not let their reward in the Hereafter go to waste.
His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe to those who deny God’s report of the honor He will bestow upon these God-fearing people on the Day of Resurrection.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; you are guilty indeed (46). Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (47). When they are told, “Bow down,” they do not bow down (48). Woe that Day to those who deny the truth (49).’ God threatens and warns those who deny resurrection: eat for the remainder of your lifespans and enjoy the remainder of your lives for a little while—you are guilty. You are following the pattern of earlier guilty nations, who were allowed to enjoy their lives until their appointed terms, then God took vengeance on them for their disbelief and denial of their messengers. Ibn Zayd said the verse refers to the people of disbelief.
His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe that Day to those who denied God’s report in this verse about what He will do to them.
His saying, ‘When they are told, “Bow down,” they do not bow down’: God says, when they are told … … these guilty people who deny God’s threat, ‘Bow down,’ they do not bow.
The interpreters differed about when this is said to them.

Some said it is in the Hereafter, when they are summoned to prostrate but cannot. Ibn ʿAbbās said they will be called to prostrate on the Day of Resurrection but will be unable, because they did not prostrate to God in this world.

Others said it was said to them in this life. Qatādah said they should be told to bow properly, for prayer holds a high place with God. He related from Ibn Masʿūd that he saw one man praying without bowing and another dragging his lower garment. Ibn Masʿūd laughed; when asked why, he said one man’s prayer would not be accepted and God would not look at the other.

Some said ‘bow’ here means pray. Mujāhid explained ‘bow down’ as ‘pray.’ Al-Ṭabarī says the most correct view is that God reports these guilty people opposed His commands and prohibitions: they did not comply with what He commanded or refrain from what He prohibited.
His saying, ‘Woe that Day to those who deny the truth’: woe to those who denied God’s messengers and rejected what they conveyed to them of His commands and prohibitions.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘In what discourse after this will they believe? (50)’ God says: people, after this Qur’an—which you have denied despite the clarity of its proof and the soundness of its evidence that it is the truth from God—what discourse will you believe? That is, what will you affirm? God informs them that if they do not affirm the reports brought by this Qur’an, despite the sound proofs establishing their truth, they will be unable to affirm other reports about matters they have neither witnessed nor seen. If they accept anything unseen on the basis of evidence, they must do the same with the reports in this Qur’an. God knows best. This is the end of the commentary on Sūrat al-Mursalāt.
